key_insight: Submesoscale frontogenesis can drive strong diapycnal tracer transport, with a major share coming from mean advective flux linked to secondary circulation rather than turbulence alone.
engineering_relevance: Ocean and climate models need to represent this multiscale frontal transport pathway to better predict vertical exchange of heat, nutrients, and pollutants.
method: Large-eddy simulation of a submesoscale frontal zone
Passive tracer transport analysis across density surfaces
Decomposition of diapycnal flux into turbulent covariance and mean advective components
evidence_signal: The abstract reports that intense turbulence forms during frontogenesis and that a substantial fraction of the resulting diapycnal tracer transport is explained by mean diapycnal advection driven by evolving secondary circulation.
watch_item: The mechanism is demonstrated in LES for an idealized frontal setup, so its magnitude and parameterization may differ in real ocean conditions.
paper_title: Diapycnal material transport driven by submesoscale frontogenesis
